respectively adverb

also in that order, each in turn, the former … the latter

classical

Lewis & Short s.v. hic: opposed to ille, “the latter … the former”

1An entry of a kind this lexicon keeps on purpose: where Latin has no equivalent, it says so and shows what Latin does instead.

hic … ille1

construction: the two demonstratives, each picking up one of two things just named

the latter … the former

Latin has no word for “respectively”. English lists two sets and adds the word to pair them off (“Marcus and Julia are five and seven respectively”); Latin pairs them in the sentence itself. With two things, hic points to the nearer, the one named last, and ille to the farther, the one named first.

Other words

  • alter … alter — the one … the other

    also used · classical

    When the order does not matter, or each half gets its own clause: alter quīnque annōs nātus est, altera septem.

  • suus quisque — each … his own

    also used · classical

    For “each to his own respective place, share or task”: suum cuique; in suam quisque domum.

Examples

  • Mārcus quīnque annōs nātus est, Jūlia septem.

    Marcus and Julia are five and seven respectively.composed

  • In suam quisque domum rediērunt.

    They went back to their respective homes.composed

See also this, that, each, the other, own.
